title: ELEPHANTS IN THE FOG: A Thriller Set in a Transgender Community in Rural Nepal - Hollywood Times
description: ELEPHANTS IN THE FOG: A Thriller Set in a Transgender Community in Rural Nepal  Hollywood Times
publisher.title: Hollywood Times
full_article:
A fascinating and unexpected film from Nepal worth seeing is Elephants in the Fog , a senstitive debut by Abinash Bikfram Shah set in the heart of Nepal’s transgender community. Winner of this year’s Un Certain Regard jury prize at Cannes, it screened at AFI FEST on October 22. Elephants in the Fog is about about the matriarch of a Kinnar community – played by newcomer Puspa Thing Lama – whose daughter goes missing whilst on patrol for wild elephants living in the surrounding forests. Elephants in the Fog is Nepal’s submission for Best International Feature Film at the Oscars in 2027.

The Kinnar community in Nepal at a ceremony with their guru, with Pirari (Puspa Thing Lama)

Set in Thori, a rural municipality of Nepal, Elephants in the Fog focuses its narrative on the local Kinnar community, made up of the matriarch Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama) and her adopted daughters. The transgender women make up their own family, despite the prejudices they face and the way they are perceived from people outside of their community in their village surrounded by wild elephants.

Matriarch Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama) and her adopted daughters dancing a wedding.

When Aspara, one of Pirati’s daughters, goes missing, her family does everything in their power to find her and get justice, while Pirati herself is torn between her duty to the community as a Kinnar and her need for personal freedom and love. Elephants in the Fog explores a community about which most viewers in the audience probably don’t know to exist and shines a light on what life really looks like from their perspective. This is true in terms of the narrative as well as behind the camera, as the actors cast in the roles of the Kinnars are transgender women.

The term Kinnar refers to a traditional third-gender, transgender, or intersex community in North India, In the 21st century, many hijras live in well-defined and organized all-hijra communities, led by a guru. Over generations, these communities have consisted of those who are in abject poverty or who have been rejected by or fled their family of origin. Today, Nepal, Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh have all legally accepted the existence of a third gender, with India, Pakistan, and Nepal including an option for them on passports and certain official documents.

Matriarch Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama) and her adopted daughter Aspara who wears a blonde wig

The Kinnars themselves and the relationships between them are the beating heart of this character-driven movie, and the driving force behind this story. The choice to film on location is also a successful one, as the film highlights the landscape of the country it is filmed in. Directed by Abinash Bikram Shuah, Elephants in the Fog is as much about the Kinnars as it is about the place in which it is set and filmed in, which is constantly present in the narrative through the beautiful cinematography by Noé Bach.

Elephants in the Fog tends to focus on Pirati, the “mother” of the Kinnar family, more than anyone else. The stories of the other Kinnars who are equally as compelling, but not developed in detail. This is true especially for Aspara who wears a blonde wig and loves dancing. We do learn that Aspara had previously worked as a sex worker for a mean-spirited pimp but asked to join Pirati’s Kinnar family, which requires celibacy and real work. That work includes performances at heterosexual weddings, where they provide blessings to the newly-weds and also bless pregnant women. We do see an induction ceremony of a new Kinnar into the community with an aged Kinnar as their guru.

Bahuchara Mata, the Hindu goddess of chastity and fertility

The Kinnars worship Bahuchara Mata, the Hindu goddess of chastity and fertility in her maiden aspect, of the incarnation of the Hinglaj. She is worshiped as a goddess of fertility, chastity, protection, and transformation. The Kinnar and Hijra communities invoke her name when bestowing blessings for newborns and newlywed couples. In regional folklore, she is associated with curing impotence, protecting those who cross traditional gender norms, and granting sacred legitimacy to third-gender roles. Although many Kinnars are also sex workers, Pirati’s “family” follows the guidance of their guru about celibacy. They perform blessings at weddings and other occasions related to fertility and child-bearing during the day, but are not supposed to be out at night. The village appreciates their good services but remains watchful of transgressions.

While tense throughout, the first act feels slower than the rest of the movie. Much of it sets up the setting as well as the key information that the audience should be aware of regarding the Kinnar community and how they are perceived and their playful moments as well as their ability to help the village farming community. Although the Kinnar family is supposed to be celibate, it turns out at Pirati has a relationship with a Nepalese man who dotes on her and often gives her rides on his bicycle. The others consider this inappropriate given Pirati’s role as a “mother.”

Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama) getting a ride on the bicycle of a Nepalese villagers who dotes on her.

Things heat up when the young wig-wearing Aspara is seen dancing with straight sex workers for a large group of young men. Pirati drags her back home and admonishes her for violating the rules of her Kinnar “family.” Aspara’s former relationship with an abusive tuktuk driver becomes the reason for Aspara’s disappearance into the forest and possibly her death. This forest in this part of southern Nepal is a dangerous place with herds of wild elephants that often enter local villages in search of food and destroy the crops. The forest of Thori village is considered sacred to the god Shiva and the elephants to be respected and feared. No one dares to go into the forest at night. However, the Kunnars seem to have a special relation to this sacred forest, as we come to see in story.

Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama) dealing with the Nepalese police over the disappearance of Aspara.

Although the Kinnars dress up scarecrows with discarded clothing of bright colors to ward off elephants, the villagers seem unable to keep the elephants from approaching the village and eating their crops. Eventually the villagers put up an electric fence to keep the elephants from entering freely at night, but its effectiveness has its limitations. The elephants come to be a symbolic mix of nature’s ways and traditional religious beliefs that determine the fascinating direction of the film.

Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama), the “mother” with her adopted daughters challenging the villagers.

Overall, Elephants in the Fog is a powerful film that shines a light on an underrepresented and misunderstood community in Nepal and the love they have for each other. Like a small handful of international films before it, Shahl’s feature debut continues the tradition established by Italian neorealism of on location shooting, non-professional actors, and focusing on the everyday people in a masterful way. In doing so, the film manages to continue the legacy of classic masterpieces like Roberto Rosselini’s Rome, Open City, Vittorio De Sica’s Bicycle Thieves, and Satyaljit Ray’s Pather Panchali.

Abinash Bikfram Shah, director of “Elephants in the Fog.”

title: Nepal becomes first country to receive climate change reparations - The Telegraph
description: Nepal becomes first country to receive climate change reparations  The Telegraph
publisher.title: The Telegraph
full_article:
Nepal has become the first country to receive climate change reparations from a new United Nations fund after deadly flash flooding earlier this year.

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage was set up in 2023 to help countries deal with climate-related disasters.

It decided on Thursday to earmark $20m (£15m) for Nepal to help it recover from the devastating flash flood of Aug 26, which killed more than 1,400 people.

It is being seen as an important institutional breakthrough towards turning a long-standing demand by developing countries affected by climate change into financial support.

However, as per the fund guidelines, the $20m is the maximum amount that can be requested for a single project.

The amount is 0.7% of the $2.7bn Nepal has estimated in losses to infrastructure and economy.

In a statement, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) described the payout as “a historic milestone for climate justice and solidarity with Nepal”.

It added: “This approval represents the very first time the Fund has moved to support a country facing a sudden-onset climate disaster since its operationalisation at COP28.”

title: How a hero principal who saved hundreds of pupils from the Nepal floods is rebuilding broken lives - The National
description: How a hero principal who saved hundreds of pupils from the Nepal floods is rebuilding broken lives  The National
publisher.title: The National
full_article:
The principal of a government school in flood-hit Nepal has set up tents to ensure hundreds of children he guided to safety two months ago can continue their education.

Rajendra Dawadi, head of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot, one of the areas hit hardest by the flash floods, was hailed as a hero when his swift actions helped to save the lives of 900 children, before a torrent of water crashed into the school compound on August 26.

He has made it his mission to enable classes to continue, using 20 tents and the shaded sections of a local sports academy. His goal is to provide some normality to families who lost their homes and livelihoods in the flooding that killed at least 1,455 people, with 5,285 listed as missing.

“People lost everything. But the children are still eager to study,” Mr Dawadi told The National. “There was a big celebration on the first day – I thought most children would not come back to the school, but more than 95 per cent came back, they cheered, they exchanged happiness.

"I was very happy. My school family, the teachers, students, their smiling faces made me more happy.”

A video from September 21 shows children cheering as classes resume in tents set up on higher ground. Mr Dawadi, 47, said it could take at least two years to rebuild the school.

As thousands across Nepal look to pick up the pieces after the disaster – which was caused by glacial ice and rock collapsing into a Himalayan river – the UN has said funding is urgently needed.

Fractured lives

The raging waters that cut through the school compound have since receded. Only the roof of a three-storey building is still visible, with the rest submerged in thick mud. Other buildings were swept away.

The devastation across six districts has left deep scars in the school. One child became an orphan and 12 pupils lost one parent.

“Many children need our support. They lost their father, some their mother,” Mr Dawadi said.

“The students had counselling sessions, music classes. We try to motivate them, we make it like a family environment in school. I tell them it was a black day but we saved our lives and had a rebirth for me, my colleagues, my students. It was a rebirth from the great disaster.”

Attendance is strong, with 1,621 pupils showing up for class. They sit on the floor in tents and share benches and desks under the stairwell of a sports centre. The tents, books and furniture were provided by Unicef and private foundations.

School authorities await a decision on new land where they can rebuild. Until then, there are other pressing matters – pupils will need a library and science labs. Two more buses are also required to help children get to lessons at the tent site.

Parents whose children had attended private schools are now sending them to free government institutions. “People are in trauma but they are doing their work, they are trying to be normal,” Mr Dawadi said. “Parents are worried about studies so they send children here, even if it’s in tents.”

Critical moments

It took only 11 minutes from the time Mr Dawadi first raised the alarm to when floodwater crashed into the school. Two school staff were killed in the flood.

Mr Dawadi was teaching when he heard two staff members shouting about heavy flooding in the nearby Rasuwa district.

The roof of one building is all that can be seen of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School. Photo: Rajendra Dawadi Show caption: The roof of one building is all that can be seen of Tribhuva…

He quickly told teachers to take pupils from each class to higher ground, urging them not to panic. Mr Dawadi turned away a bus with young children that was entering the compound and anther bus was also alerted about the danger.

Older pupils who had motorbikes and bicycles were asked to help take other children to safety. “People were saying, 'Flood, flood,' but the sun was shining here,” he recalled. “But I decided to close the school. First, I told my staff to ring the bell. Then I told class teachers to go to separate classes to say school is off due to the flood, to go to a safer place … three girls fainted. When we left the school, the water had already entered. It was 11 minutes.”

But Mr Dawadi praised his staff. “I am not the real hero,” he said. “My team worked together, this was my duty. For this, I was recognised all over the world.”

Heart of community

The school is a vital part of the community and parents have welcomed the return of classes.

“We had tears in our eyes when school started – all parents felt it,” said Sharmila Shreshtha, 46, whose home and stationery shop were destroyed in the disaster. “We have nothing. Our homes are gone, our shop is gone, we are so tired. But the school makes everyone happy.”

Some classes are conducted under the stairwell at a sports academy. Photo: Rajendra Dawadi Show caption: Some classes are conducted under the stairwell at a sports a…

Pupils have appealed for books, computers and lab equipment. Aspiring software engineer Saswot Shah, 14, worries about how a lack of equipment will affect his studies.

"Earlier we had smartboards, computers, maths and science laboratories. Now we are just surviving. We work together but we need a proper computer and maths lab,” he said.

Pradakshina Shreshtha, 16, lost her home and now lives in rented accommodation. She hopes to be a doctor, but worries about exams.

Nepal Flood Relief Continues; Field Medic Packs Reach the Philippines and Panama

By Tori Gordon

Over the past week, Direct Relief sent 571 shipments of requested medical aid, containing 15.2 million defined daily doses of medication, to organizations across 48 U.S. states and territories and 18 other countries.

Shipments sent this week included respiratory treatments, cancer therapies, rare disease therapies, and cold-chain equipment.

Medical Camp Brings Specialist Care to Flood-Affected Communities in Nepal

Mountain Heart Nepal, in collaboration with WOREC Nepal, organized a multidisciplinary medical camp for communities still recovering from flooding and landslides, with essential medicines donated by Direct Relief supporting the effort. More than 250 patients received care with access to general medicine, specialist care, and psychosocial counseling, services that would otherwise require significant travel.

Women also received cervical cancer screening, and women and adolescent girls took part in sessions on reproductive health.

"Specialist doctors and health workers need to reach people's doorsteps," said Dr. Ram Thapa Chhetri, Mountain Heart Nepal's camp coordinator. "Camps like this also let us screen for diseases that have gone unrecognised for a long time, find them early and refer people for treatment."

Mountain Heart Nepal also handed over three emergency medical backpacks to strengthen local emergency response capacity, two to Gajuri Rural Municipality and one to the Nepal Army's Shree Bhairav Gan, stationed in Gajuri, to support frontline medical response during future emergencies.

Volunteers Assemble 100 Field Medic Packs in the Philippines

Direct Relief partner Philippine Disaster Resilience Foundation, or PDRF, hosted a packing event at its Operations Center in Clark, Philippines, where 20 student and youth volunteers from the University of the Philippines, Clark, spent three hours assembling 100 field medic packs. The initial 20 bags will go to newly trained emergency medical responders from PDRF partner communities across the country.

The event comes as the Philippines faces the dual threat of severe tropical cyclones during typhoon season and challenges posed by El NiÃ±o. Creating a strategic stockpile in the Philippines, which regularly ranks among the most disaster-prone nations in the world, allows responders to deploy quickly when disaster strikes.

"We're very happy we have this very strong partnership with Direct Relief," said Arnel Capili, Operations Center Director at PDRF. "Through the prepositioning of these emergency response bags, we're able to make sure that our responders are able to be deployed in a very timely manner so that we can make a difference in the lives of those who are affected by disasters in the Philippines."

Pre-Positioned Supplies Support Panama Earthquake Response

The Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, delivered 20 field medic packs donated by Direct Relief to Panama's Ministry of Health this month, supporting health teams responding to the magnitude 7.7 earthquake that struck the country's Azuero Peninsula on Oct. 9. The backpacks, distributed through the Los Santos Health Region, were drawn from Direct Relief inventory prepositioned at PAHO's regional strategic reserve warehouse in Panama City, designed to help health workers reach communities and shelters where access to care may be limited.

"Following an earthquake, it is essential to bring health care closer to communities and shelters," said Lilian Reneau GaitÃ¡n, PAHO/WHO Representative a.i. in Panama.

Having supplies like hurricane preparedness packs and emergency backpacks pre-positioned with PAHO in Panama allows for a quick regional response, a model that has supported past emergencies including the earthquakes in Venezuela earlier this year and Hurricane Melissa's impact on Jamaica and Haiti last year.

full_article:
The Board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), a UN body, has unanimously agreed to provide $21.6 million (around ₹ 205 crore) to flood-ravaged Nepal.

The extraordinary board meeting on October 22 decided to “provisionally set aside an additional $21.6 million, including $1.6 million for oversight fee”.

Climate experts consider the step to be a historical one as this is the first time the fund has responded to a request for support in the aftermath of an immediate climate-induced loss and damage event. They, however, called for a permanent mechanism for responding to such climate-inflicted urgency.

A September 2026 analysis by scientists and glaciologists associated with the World Weather Attribution found that human-induced warming, which pushed up the freezing level in the mountains by around 100 metres per decade and led to glacier thinning and thawing of permafrost, had caused the catastrophic flood in Nepal on August 26.

The Telegraph had on September 13 reported that the co-chairpersons of the board, set up by the UN to help developing countries cope with climate change-triggered losses, had assured financial support to the Nepal government.

Nepal’s finance minister Swarnim Wagle and agriculture, forests and environment minister Gita Chaudhary had, in a letter on August 31, requested urgent support from the fund.

According to sources, the Nepal government estimates the initial economic loss and damage from the floods at ₹ 2.69 billion, with the initial recovery and reconstruction needs at ₹ 4.71 billion. “This is notwithstanding the irreparable non-economic losses linked to the disaster,” said an expert based in Nepal.

“The Loss and Damage Fund took a historic first step by responding to Nepal, but this cannot be a one-off. No country should have to endure a catastrophe and wait seven weeks just to unlock the fund’s first-ever emergency meeting. We must set up a permanent rapid-response system that moves support in days, not months,” said Harjeet Singh, a climate expert and the global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign.

“Developed countries bowed to the pressure and backed setting aside $20 million for Nepal. But even as they did, they kept insisting it must not set a precedent. They continue to shy away from the hundreds of billions of dollars that vulnerable countries actually need to respond to loss and damage,” Singh said.

KATHMANDU: Economic Digest presents a brief yet comprehensive roundup of major business developments in Nepal, delivered in clear and accessible summaries.

Recent developments in Nepal highlight the government’s efforts to strengthen regional diplomacy, expand financial access, improve public administration and address climate-related vulnerabilities. Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle’s engagement with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and other Indian leaders at the NDTV World Summit underscores the importance of Nepal–India relations, particularly in economic cooperation and regional stability.

International climate financing has also gained significance, with the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage agreeing to allocate USD 20 million for flood recovery. However, the requirement for a detailed project proposal highlights the need for effective planning and implementation. Similarly, UNFPA’s climate-resilient healthcare model in Rautahat demonstrates how targeted infrastructure investment and qualified health workers can protect essential services during disasters.

In the financial sector, collateral-free digital loans and the restoration of banking services reflect expanding digital access and the growing importance of cybersecurity. Meanwhile, the Supreme Court’s ruling on demonetized Indian banknotes clarifies the legal interpretation of foreign exchange offenses. The government’s concessional vehicle loan scheme for public officials, however, raises questions about fiscal priorities and equitable use of public resources.

Tourism recovery in Myagdi and Mustang indicates renewed economic activity following monsoon disruptions, while rising traffic congestion exposes infrastructure and mobility challenges. Overall, these developments underscore the need to balance economic growth, institutional accountability, disaster resilience and sustainable development through coordinated policies and effective implementation.

Finance Minister Wagle meets Indian PM Modi at NDTV World Summit

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi briefly in New Delhi on Thursday evening during the NDTV World Summit 2026, following a major address by the Indian leader. Wagle arrived in the Indian capital on Thursday as an invited international speaker and delivered a special session titled “Prosperity through Proximity: India–Nepal Opportunity” at Hotel Taj Palace. During the visit, he also took part in a session featuring Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar. The discussions focused on the evolving global order, bilateral ties and opportunities for economic cooperation between Nepal and India.

FRLD allocates $20 million for flood recovery in Nepal

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) has agreed to allocate USD 20 million (approximately Rs 3.26 billion) to assist recovery and reconstruction efforts in Nepal’s flood-hit areas. The decision follows Nepal’s appeal for emergency support after devastating floods struck the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river region on August 26, resulting in fatalities and widespread destruction. However, the allocation does not mean the funds have already been released. Nepal must first submit a detailed project proposal for review and approval before the money can be disbursed. The decision is an important step towards obtaining international assistance for climate-related disasters, although the amount covers only part of Nepal’s overall recovery and reconstruction requirements.

Eleven banks offer collateral-free phone loans of up to Rs 200,000

Eleven commercial banks in Nepal are offering collateral-free digital loans, known as Phone Loan, allowing eligible customers to borrow up to Rs 200,000 directly through mobile banking applications without submitting physical documents or pledging assets. The participating banks are Everest Bank, Nabil Bank, NIC Asia Bank, NMB Bank, Citizens Bank, Kumari Bank, Laxmi Sunrise Bank, Machhapuchhre Bank, Prabhu Bank, Rastriya Banijya Bank and Agriculture Development Bank. Borrowing limits are determined automatically by system algorithms that assess customers’ account transaction histories over the preceding six months. Although repayment periods generally span one year, some banks offer terms of up to two years, providing greater flexibility for salaried customers and regular depositors.

Supreme Court rules demonetized Indian notes cannot establish foreign exchange offenses

The Supreme Court has ruled that demonetized foreign banknotes that no longer hold legal tender status in their country of origin cannot serve as the legal basis for establishing offenses under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1962. The ruling overturned earlier court decisions in a case stemming from July 17, 2018, when authorities seized Rs 5.3 million worth of demonetized Indian banknotes from a hotel in Rupandehi. The apex court observed that once the issuing monetary authority withdraws a currency’s legal tender status, the notes lose their essential characteristics as money. Consequently, possession of invalidated banknotes does not, by itself, amount to an illegal foreign exchange transaction. The full text of the verdict was released on July 30, 2026.

Government introduces concessional vehicle loans of up to Rs 6 million for public officials

The government has introduced a concessional loan scheme for public employees to purchase official vehicles under the Government Employees Vehicle Management Guideline, 2026, with the government covering the full interest cost. Loan ceilings vary according to administrative rank, with chief secretaries and secretaries eligible for up to Rs 6 million, joint secretaries Rs 5 million, and under-secretaries Rs 4 million. Section officers can receive up to Rs 400,000 to purchase two-wheelers, while non-gazetted employees are eligible for up to Rs 200,000. Repayment periods may extend to 20 years. Officials who choose to drive their vehicles themselves instead of using assigned institutional drivers will also receive an additional cash allowance equivalent to the standard salary of a driver.

Traffic congestion rises at major entry points to Kathmandu Valley

Traffic congestion has intensified at major entry points to the Kathmandu Valley as people return home after the festive holidays. Authorities have reported increased vehicle movement along key routes, including Nagdhunga–Kalanki, Jadibuti–Koteshwor, Tinpipale, Jagati, Bhattedanda and Dakshinkali–Farping. Traffic police have been deployed to manage the flow of vehicles and reduce the risk of road accidents. Daily traffic at major checkpoints currently averages around 1,000 vehicles. Official records show that 79,676 vehicles carried 576,578 people out of the capital between Ghatasthapana and October 20 for the annual festivities. The continuing return of holiday travellers is expected to keep major highways and entry routes busy in the coming days.

Machhapuchhre Bank and Nabil Bank restore full digital banking services

Machhapuchhre Bank and Nabil Bank have announced the full restoration of their web-based platforms, mobile banking services and other digital banking facilities following temporary suspensions. The interruptions were linked to system upgrades undertaken in response to global software vulnerabilities and broader security assessments. Bank officials said technical reviews and security enhancements had been completed to protect customer information and financial transaction systems. With the maintenance work finished, previously unavailable services—including debit card requests, credit card applications and secured loan processing—are operational again for retail and corporate customers across Nepal.

Tourist arrivals pick up in Myagdi and Mustang after festive holidays

Tourism activity is recovering in Myagdi and nearby destinations following the festive holidays, helped by favorable weather and the reopening of the Beni–Jomsom highway after the monsoon season. Local businesses have reported a steady flow of visitors to popular attractions, including Ghorepani, Poon Hill, Khopara, Singa Tatopani, Bhurung–Tatopani, Annapurna Base Camp, Rupse and Galeshwar. Travel had been severely affected by heavy monsoon flooding along the Kaligandaki river corridor during the second-to-last week of September. However, road clearance work completed late last month has restored vehicle access to the affected areas. Poon Hill, situated at an altitude of 3,210 metres, and nearby trekking routes continue to draw domestic and international visitors. Around 150 domestic tourists have reportedly departed for base camp excursions.

More than 700 foreign tourists enter Mustang via Thorong La Pass after snow clearance

A total of 772 foreign tourists have entered Mustang over the past two weeks after crossing Thorong La Pass from Besisahar through Manang, following operations to clear snow from the route. Records maintained by the Annapurna Conservation Area Project checkpoint in Jomsom show that the arrivals included 43 visitors from South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) member countries and 729 from other nations. The pass, located at an altitude of 5,416 metres along the Annapurna Circuit trekking route, is exposed to severe seasonal weather conditions. Joint efforts by local tourism entrepreneurs and security personnel helped clear the snow and reopen the trail. Tourism representatives said more than 100 trekkers are crossing the pass daily towards Muktinath, with high-altitude trekking expected to continue until the end of November.

UNFPA introduces scalable model for climate-resilient healthcare in Rautahat

The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) has established a model for climate-resilient maternal and newborn healthcare in Nepal, demonstrating how frontline health facilities can maintain life-saving services during severe climate-related disasters. The model was highlighted during a policy dialogue and field visit to the Auraiya Birthing Centre in Ishnath Municipality, Madhesh Province. The event brought together government representatives, healthcare providers and community leaders to review successful adaptation measures and chart a roadmap for scaling up climate-resilient health infrastructure in other vulnerable regions of Nepal, according to a UNFPA press release issued today. During an official visit to the centre, United Nations Resident Coordinator in Nepal Lila Pieters Yahia said even small, targeted investments could significantly improve access to maternal healthcare. “My visit to Auraiya Birthing Centre showed me how even small, targeted investments can make a real difference in access to maternal healthcare. What struck me most was the importance of having a qualified nurse at the health post. Her presence has built trust in the community, giving rural women, including those in more conservative communities, the confidence to seek care during pregnancy and after childbirth,” she said.
